head:
Core · Measurement

Why a standardised test beats how you feel

In the article “Measure to improve: training is not enough”, the question was whether to measure at all. Here we assume you do, and ask the next question: how do you measure so that the number is worth something? A test taken any old way, on a good day or a tired one, with or without a warm-up, gives a number. That number does not necessarily tell you what you think it does. We will see why test protocols are so strict, and what has to be fixed each time you take the test.

The problem

A test protocol often looks excessive. Walking exactly six minutes along a 30-metre corridor, with encouraging phrases planned in advance. Squeezing a dynamometer while seated, elbow at a right angle, three times. It feels like a ceremony. Each of us more or less knows whether we are “in shape”: so what is the point?

The intuitive answer is that how you feel is enough, and that a test only confirms it with a number. But even when you measure, a number can be bad. It can vary simply because you drank a coffee, because the track was shorter, or because someone else was shouting encouragement at you. If that is the case, an improvement in your score might be nothing but noise, and a drop nothing but a bad day.

The question

What does a standardised test give you that your feeling, or a test taken in a rush, does not, and what has to be fixed so that two results are truly comparable?

What is at stake

Four things depend on the answer.

Your training decisions. If you set your load, your pace or your volume from a number, that number has to be right. A false improvement makes you keep a programme that does not work. A false decline makes you change one that did.

Your health. Cardiorespiratory fitness and grip strength are followed in medicine because they are linked to future health. Tracking how they change only makes sense if two successive measurements are comparable.

Your mindset. If a gap comes from the time of day of the test, you are motivated or discouraged for nothing.

Your comparison with others. A norm table by age and sex is only worth something if your test was taken in the same way as the one used to build the table.

These stakes cannot be left unanswered. The demonstration that follows goes from the general to the specific, in six steps.

  1. What a feeling of effort is worth, compared with a measurement.
  2. What statements about what we do are worth, compared with a device.
  3. A standardised test, repeated, gives almost the same number.
  4. But the second attempt is not the first: day-to-day variability and the learning effect.
  5. What moves the number: the tester, the position, the course, the time of day, the encouragement.
  6. The smallest detectable change, what it lets you compare, and the objections.
rest:
Step 1 of 6The feeling of effort is useful, but it cannot be compared from one day to the next

Claim: perceived effort tracks intensity well within a single effort, but it is not very stable when repeated.

The most widely used tool for putting a number on perceived effort is the Borg scale. The classic scale runs from 6 (no effort) to 20 (absolute maximum), and a shorter version runs from 0 to 10.2 You might think it is worthless. It is not. In 2,560 men and women who took progressive tests on a treadmill or bike, perceived effort correlated with heart rate (r = 0.74) and with blood lactate (r = 0.83). The authors conclude that this holds regardless of sex, age, activity level or the presence of coronary artery disease.1 A correlation of 1 would mean the two measures move exactly together, and a correlation of 0 that they have nothing to do with each other. A meta-analysis in healthy people, cited by a rehabilitation reference centre, gives more modest correlations for heart rate, from 0.47 to 0.61.2

What these numbers mean for you: your feeling is a good indicator for setting a pace during a session. It is real information, and no test replaces it.

The question changes when you want to compare two days. A Spanish team had 15 amateur runners, 34 years old on average, run a Cooper test (running as far as possible in 12 minutes on a 400-metre track) twice, 48 hours apart, in similar weather conditions, after a 15-minute warm-up.3 The runners covered almost the same distance: 3,026 metres, then 3,047 metres. Their maximum heart rate was almost identical too: 182 then 183 beats per minute. But their perceived effort, rated from 0 to 10, went from 8.7 to 9.5 on average, a significant difference.

For the same effort repeated, distance and heart rate repeat, perceived effort far less so

Intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) between two Cooper tests 48 hours apart, with its 95% confidence interval (black line). 15 amateur male runners. Source: Alvero-Cruz et al., Revista Andaluza de Medicina del Deporte, 2017.3

What this means

The ICC measures whether people keep their place and their value from one attempt to the next: 1 is perfect agreement, 0 none. Distance (0.99) and heart rate (0.93) repeat almost identically. Perceived effort drops to 0.68, with an interval that goes down to 0.05: with 15 people, we cannot rule out that it is very unstable. The authors question its use for tracking change in this context. For you: how you feel can tell you “that was hard”, but it cannot tell you “that was easier than two months ago”.

This study is small, but the scale's information sheet adds that its instructions must not be shortened and that 5 to 10% of adults misunderstand the instruction.2 So perceived effort depends on how it is asked, and it moves even when the effort does not.

There is another way to do without a test: saying what you do.

Step 2 of 6What we say we do differs from what a device records

Claim: relying on your own statements gives very variable numbers, in both directions.

A systematic review compared, in the scientific literature, measures of physical activity reported by people (questionnaires, diaries) with direct measures. Of 4,463 articles identified in eight databases, 187 had their data extracted.4 The result is not what you would expect. Reported values were sometimes higher than the direct measure, sometimes lower, with no clear pattern. And the agreement between the two, measured by a correlation, was generally low to moderate, with values ranging from -0.71 to 0.96.4

Between what we report and what a device measures, the link ranges from negative to almost perfect

Range of correlations between reported and direct measurement of physical activity in adults, from one study to another. The range gives the extremes; according to the review, values are generally low to moderate. Source: systematic review by Prince and colleagues, International Journal of Behavioral Nutrition and Physical Activity, 2008.4

What this means

A correlation of -0.71 would mean that, in that study, those who reported the most were those the device measured the least. 0.96 would mean almost perfect agreement. Between the two, the method decides the result. For you: what you think you did this week is not a reliable reference for assessing yourself or setting your load. The authors note that the method can noticeably change the observed level of activity.

The classic form of the problem is believing we are more active than we are. For the level of an entire population, this is what US surveys show: reported levels are higher than levels measured by accelerometer.5 The analysis of the national study by Troiano and colleagues, based on the accelerometer, concludes that adherence to the recommendations is clearly lower than what the self-reports give.6 Only the abstract of this study could be read, without its percentages: they are not quoted here. The review, for its part, adds nuance: at the level of individuals, the gap goes in both directions.

These two steps dealt with perceptions, informative but poorly calibrated. Let us look at a test with fixed rules: its first quality should be to give the same number again when nothing has changed.

Step 3 of 6Taken by the rules, a test gives almost the same number again

Claim: a test with a fixed protocol is reproducible, including for simple measures such as the 12-minute run, the 6-minute walk or grip strength.

This is test-retest reliability: you take the same test twice, in people whose condition has not changed, and see whether the result is found again.

The Cooper test first: we saw above an ICC of 0.99 for distance, in 15 runners.3 Another study, in 60 young adults who had each taken two field tests (Cooper and shuttle) three times, finds a reliability coefficient of 0.96 for these tests.14

Then grip strength. One group tested 114 adults from 17 to over 66 years old, on two consecutive days, at the same time, with the same protocol: seated, feet on the floor, three maximal contractions of about 5 seconds, standardised encouragement and no feedback on results. The overall ICC is 0.95.7 It is a preprint, not peer reviewed, and the source shows inconsistencies in the number of trials retained. Another group measured 130 adults aged 50 to 89 at two visits a median of 88 days apart: the ICC for mean strength is 0.956.8 About three months apart, and the measurement is found again.

Finally the 6-minute walk: in 201 asthmatic patients, the ICC between two attempts is 0.91.9

Four simple tests, four measurements that are found again from one attempt to the next

Test-retest ICC. The axis starts at 0.5. Black line: 95% confidence interval when the source gives it. Different populations and intervals: amateur runners (Alvero-Cruz 2017), 114 adults (preprint), 123 adults at 88 days (Hrb Open Research), 201 asthmatic patients (Pulmonology).3,7,8,9

What this means

These ICCs lie between 0.91 and 0.99, whereas perceived effort is at 0.68. When the protocol is kept, the measurement is found again: this is the first reason to standardise. Do not draw too much from it: the ICC mainly says that the test ranks people in the same way from one attempt to the next. It does not say by how much a given person can move between two attempts. The next step shows this.

These measures are good on average. Let us look at what happens to one specific person, from one day to the next.

Step 4 of 6Good group reliability does not prevent a second attempt from differing from the first

Claim: from one day to the next, an individual moves, and the second attempt is on average better than the first.

The study of the 201 asthmatic patients shows this well. The mean distance went from 392 to 410 metres between the first and second test, 18 metres more (5%), a significant difference. 73% of patients walked further the second time. 39% gained at least 27 metres, the smallest difference judged important in asthma. And 11% lost at least 27 metres.9 The authors speak of a considerable learning effect and recommend at least two tests per person.

Of 100 patients, 73 walk further the second time, but 11 walk clearly less

Change in distance between a first and a second 6-minute walk test, 201 asthmatic patients. 73%, 39% and 11% are given by the source. 34% (73 minus 39) and 16% (the remainder) are calculated. Source: reliability study of the 6-minute walk test in asthma, Pulmonology, 2022.9

What this means

If you take the test once and retake it two months later, part of your “improvement” may come simply from having already done the test: you know the course, you pace yourself better, you are less apprehensive. Conversely, about one person in ten drops clearly without anything else in this study to attribute it to besides day-to-day variability. A single number is not enough to conclude.

The same phenomenon exists elsewhere. In the joint European and American respiratory societies' guideline on walking tests, summarised by a review, the second 6-minute walk is on average 26 metres longer in patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. The recommendation is to do two, at least 30 minutes apart, with heart rate back to resting, and to keep the best distance.10 In children aged 7 to 9, grip strength gains 0.50 kg on average between two consecutive days, which the authors link to learning or motivation.11

These results come from patients and children: they show a mechanism, not the size of the effect in you. If the second attempt differs, what else moves the number?

Step 5 of 6Test conditions move the number

Claim: the tester, the position, the course, the encouragement and the time of day change the result, sometimes more than what the test is trying to measure.

The Irish study on grip strength (130 adults, two visits) is precise on this point, because it separated the effects. For the non-dominant hand: the morning measurement is 0.83 kg lower, the first contraction is stronger than the second by 0.87 kg, and the repeat visit is 0.71 kg higher. The largest effect is that of the person administering the test: changing the tester shifts the results by 1.10 to 1.95 kg.8 Time of day, for its part, has no clear effect on mean and maximum strength, which shows that a factor we think is important is not always as important as we think.

Simply changing the person who measures shifts the result by more than a kilo

Grip strength gaps (kg) by condition, 130 adults aged 50 to 89: non-dominant hand for time of day, order of trials and repeat visit, all measures combined for the tester. The dotted line is the minimal detectable change at 95% of mean strength (5.66 kg). The tester effect is given as a range of 1.10 to 1.95 kg depending on the measures. Source: grip strength reliability study in the TILDA cohort, HRB Open Research, 2020.8

What this means

Each of these gaps is small compared with the minimal change of 5.66 kg. The study did not add them up, but nothing suggests they cancel out: another tester, another time and another order of trials can all pull in the same direction. What you do not control is paid for in noise, and the noise does not show in the number.

Position matters too, and in a particular way: it changes the level, not the reliability. In a study from Erasmus University in Rotterdam on grip strength, four ways of holding the arm were compared, in 16 healthy people and 8 people whose hand was affected. Repeatability was high with each, with no clear difference. But the strength values differed significantly from one protocol to another, and the one in which people were invited to exceed their previous effort gave the highest values.12 A 2021 study in 201 young adults tested lying down finds the same principle: with the elbow extended, the number is higher than with the elbow bent, by about 1.5 pounds on average (about 0.7 kg, converted).13

This point is central. A test can be perfectly reproducible and give a number that cannot be compared with that of another protocol. This is exactly what happens with the choice of test: in the study of 60 young adults, the shuttle predicted a lower aerobic capacity than the laboratory measurement, whereas the Cooper mean did not deviate from it, though with an underestimate in the least fit and an overestimate in the fittest.14 Two different tests do not give the same number, even when both are reproducible.

The course plays in the same way. For the 6-minute walk, the European and American guideline asks for a flat, straight corridor of at least 30 metres, with encouragement spoken identically every 60 seconds, and no treadmill: the treadmill gives clearly lower distances, and a very short course lowers them clearly.10 For the Cooper, a reference page indicates that reliability depends on prior training, pace and motivation.15

What remains is to know from what gap we can say that something has changed.

Step 6 of 6The smallest detectable change tells you when a gap is real, and the objections tell you where rigour stops

Claim: every test has a margin of noise, and we only speak of change beyond that margin, which is smaller the more the protocol is kept.

The smallest detectable change

Researchers call “minimal detectable change” (or “smallest real difference”) the gap below which a real change cannot be distinguished from measurement noise. A few values, all from studies where the protocol was fixed.

In the Cooper test, the variation between two attempts is 52.2 metres, or 1.7% of the mean distance: the authors specify that smaller changes should not be attributed to training or detraining.3 For grip strength, the Irish study gives 5.66 kg for mean strength.8 In children aged 10 to 13, the smallest real difference is 2.16 kg, or 9.6% of strength; in those aged 7 to 9, 2.05 kg, or 15.5%.11 For the 6-minute walk in asthmatic patients, it is 98 metres.9

Depending on the test, it takes a gap of under 2% to about 25% to say that something has changed

Minimal detectable change (95%) relative to the mean score. 1.7% (Cooper), 9.6% and 15.5% (grip strength, children) are given by the sources. About 25% for the 6-minute walk is calculated: 98 m divided by the mean of the first test (392 m). Very different populations: adult runners, non-athletic children, asthmatic patients.3,9,11

What this means

A result that moves by 3% on a Cooper test exceeds the noise in that study, whereas a result that moves by 3% on a 6-minute walk cannot be distinguished from chance in another. The rule is not the same for every test, and it only holds if you take the test in the same conditions as in the study. For you: before celebrating or worrying about a gap, compare it with the noise margin of your test.

This is what makes results comparable over time: with a constant protocol, the noise stays of the same order, and a gap that exceeds it becomes informative. It is also what makes them comparable between people: a norm table only makes sense if everyone takes the same test, in the same position, with the same instruction.

The objections

“The numbers show tests are already reliable, so why bother?” Because these reliabilities were measured with a protocol that was kept: same time of day, same instructions, repeated trials.7,8,10 They are the result of the protocol, not a property of the test.

“The values come from different populations.” Yes, and that is a limit: amateur runners, asthmatic patients, children, adults aged 50 to 89. No study read groups these tests on the same population or on this site's audience.

“The further you move from the simple number, the less reliable it is.” That is true. In 10 people, hand strength remains very reproducible (ICC of 0.96 to 0.98), but the asymmetry between hands, a number calculated from two measurements, is less so (ICC of 0.82, with an interval of 0.43 to 0.95), and the authors note that posture and hand position play a part.16 A score derived from several measurements accumulates their noise.

What remains uncertain. No study read compares, in the same people, a test taken by the rules and the same test taken without rules, with a measure of the drift. The effects described (tester, time of day, position) isolate one factor at a time: the cumulative effect of a “loose” protocol is not quantified.

The answer to the problem

The question was: what does a standardised test give that how you feel, or a test done in a rush, does not, and what has to be fixed to compare two results? Here is the answer, with its level of certainty.

What is solid. Perceived effort tracks the intensity of an effort well but repeats poorly from one attempt to the next: ICC of 0.68, against 0.99 for distance, in a small study.3 Reports of activity deviate from direct measures, in both directions, with correlations from -0.71 to 0.96.4 Tests with a fixed protocol repeat with ICCs of 0.91 to 0.99.3,7,8,9 A second attempt is on average better than the first, and some individuals deviate clearly.9,10 The tester and the position move the result, and a change of protocol changes the level measured without changing reliability.8,12,13

What is probable. The noise margins (1.7% to about 25% depending on the test and the population) give the order of magnitude of a change worth taking seriously. They have not been measured on this site's audience.

What is not demonstrated. The exact weight of each condition (warm-up, sleep, meals, weather) on each test. The ideal interval between two attempts. The total effect of a protocol that is not kept.

So, to answer: a standardised test is not more “true” than how you feel. It is more repeatable, and that is what lets you read a gap. Without a protocol, you do not know whether you are comparing your body or your test conditions.

What to put in place

Here is what has to be fixed at each test, from the element best supported by the sources to the one least supported.

  1. The person measuring and the instruction.The same tester if possible, the same words, the same encouragement at the same rhythm (every 60 seconds for the 6-minute walk). In the Irish study, changing the tester is the largest effect measured on grip strength.8,10
  2. The equipment, the position and the course.The same device set up in the same way, the same posture (for grip strength: seated, feet on the floor, elbow at 90°, forearm neutral), the same course (flat, straight, at least 30 metres for the walk, a track for the Cooper), never a treadmill in place of the field.7,10,13
  3. The timing.The same time of day, and no intense effort in the 2 hours before the test.10 In the Irish study, time of day matters little for mean strength, but it plays a role for one hand: better to fix it.8
  4. The warm-up.The same duration, the same content. The protocols read include one (15 minutes in the Cooper study and in the grip strength study).3,7 Its own effect has not been measured in the sources read: it is fixed as a precaution, not on evidence.
  5. The trials.The same number of trials, the same rest between trials, the same rule for what is kept (best or mean). For tests where you move, do a first familiarisation attempt: the international guideline asks for two 6-minute walks, at least 30 minutes apart, and keeps the best.10
  6. The pace and the motivation.The same starting strategy, the same degree of effort asked: “the maximum”. Motivation and pace influence the reliability of the Cooper.15
  7. The recorded conditions.Time, place, equipment, tester, warm-up, sleep, meals. The sources ask for the test conditions to be recorded.10,15 Sleep and meals are not quantified in the studies read: note them so you can explain a gap, not to correct it.
  8. The reading.First do two attempts at the start to see your own noise. Only speak of progress beyond your test's margin. As for spacing, nothing in the sources gives an ideal interval: it is a practical choice, for example one test every few weeks rather than every week, not an established result.

The THW test on this page gives you a number, and the protocol that follows it is the way to make it comparable. It does not replace medical advice: chest pain or abnormal breathlessness during the test are reasons to stop and to ask for it.

What these figures do not say
  • The studies cited cover different populations: 15 amateur runners, 201 asthmatic patients, 306 children, adults aged 50 to 89. None reproduces this site's audience.3,8,9,11
  • The Cooper study covers 15 people, and the grip strength study in 114 adults is a preprint.3,7
  • The review on reported activity mixes very different methods, and 38% of the studies have a lower quality score.4 Only the abstract of the Troiano study was read.6
  • No study read shows that standardising a test makes you improve: the argument concerns the quality of the measurement, not its effects.

Frequently asked questions

So is how I feel worth nothing?

It is worth a lot for setting an effort during a session: it tracks heart rate and lactate.1 It is worth little for comparing two days.3

Do I really have to take the test twice?

For walking tests, the international guideline asks for it, because the second attempt is on average better.9,10 For the others, it is a simple way to see your own margin, though no source requires it.

Can my own method be enough?

Yes, provided you never change it: an identical protocol from one time to the next makes your results comparable with each other. It will not make them comparable with a norm table built with another protocol.12

What to take from this

How you feel is for setting effort, a standardised test is for comparing. The rigour of a protocol removes from the number what is not you.
